newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Big Three automakers' Q1 net seen higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Big Three automakers' Q1 net seen higher.

text.p: The Big Three U.S. automakers are expected to post stronger first quarter earnings in the next two weeks, due largely to higher production and easy year-ago comparisons.

General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp are expected to earn a combined $3.8 billion from continuing operations in the January-March period, up from $2.4 billion in the first quarter of 1996, Burnham Securities analyst David Healy estimated.

The year-ago first quarter included a 17-day strike at two GM brake plants in Ohio, which paralyzed the automaker's North American production and reduced its net income for the period by $900 million.
And Ford's first quarter 1996 earnings suffered from heavy product launch costs for the Escort small car, the F-Series pickup truck and Taurus and Sable mid-size cars.

Chrysler is the only one of the Big Three with a "clean" comparison, but analysts said a six percent increase in production, along with a heavier concentration of pickup trucks, sport utility vehicles and minivans will help Chrysler improve its earnings for the period.

According to analysts polled by First Call Corp., Chrysler is expected to report earnings of $1.43 a share in the first quarter, compared to $1.31 a year ago. It plans to report its results on Thursday.

GM's earnings due on April 14 are expected to more than double to $2.06 a share from $0.94 in the strike-affected first quarter of 1996, while Ford on April 16 is expected to report profits of $0.86 a share, up from $0.53 a year ago.
"It looks to be a pretty reasonable quarter," said Dean Witter Reynolds Inc analyst Kenneth Blaschke. "In what looks to be a continued sloppy market, the autos are looking reasonably attractive."

Healy said the most dramatic improvment will be at GM, which earned North American margins at $350 to $400 higher than strike-adjusted year-ago levels, reflecting cost cutting and the efficiencies in producing newly redesigned car models.
But he cautioned that GM's first quarter overseas margins could be $500 per vehicle lower than last year due to a bigger mix of smaller cars and fierce price competition in Europe.

Ford is now reaping the benefits of full production of its F-Series full-size pickup trucks, as well as the new Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle, which it did not produce in the first quarter of 1996.
But tough conditions in Europe and Ford's continued struggles in rebuilding its Brazilian operations are expected to hold Ford's overseas results near breakeven levels.

Although U.S. car and truck sales for the first quarter have exceeded industry estimates, analysts warn that intensifying price competition could cause Big Three profits to weaken in the second half of the year, particularly if Japanese automakers continue to gain market share in the intermediate passenger car and small sport utility segments.
Japanese automakers gained nearly two percentage points of market share in the first quarter while the Big Three lost 2.5 percentage points.
While the Japanese gains, due in part to the strength of the dollar versus the yen, did not affect first quarter Big Three production schedules, they have begun to affect second quarter production.

Ford, for example, this week is idling four small and intermediate car plants to bring dealer inventories back into line with demand. The move will reduce Ford's North American production for the week by about 13,600 cars.
